item.title: The $1 trillion Meta trial that wasn’t
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: Meta’s settlement of a major teen social media addiction case is probably exactly what the company wanted.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: Yesterday, Meta settled a landmark trial around teen social media addiction—and it might be popping champagne right about now. The settlement lets Meta avoid a drastic redesign of its apps and could potentially give it an edge over rivals. The cherry on top: Meta gets to paint itself as an industry leader on protecting kids—while pushing much of the onus onto parents.

What happened: Perhaps the biggest sign that this was a positive outcome for Meta: Its stock immediately rallied after the news broke. The social media giant has agreed to pay about $12.7 billion to the 47 states that joined the settlement agreement (plus a separate $1 billion payment to Texas)—and could cough up about $5 billion more if TikTok, YouTube, and Snap agree to some of the safety measures Meta will now be bound to.

Whichever amount it ends up paying is just a tiny slice of the company’s annual profit last year ($60.4 billion)—and it’ll be paid over 10 years. Reminder: Meta was telling the world that states were seeking as much as $1.4 trillion—an amount that’s a whole lot more than $18 billion, but would have been ruinous for the company considering its market cap is…$1.4 trillion. (Though it still faces other litigation around teen safety.)

Meanwhile, even the restrictions Meta agreed to implement don’t go far enough, critics say. And the big elephant in the room: If teen social media bans around the world are any indication, underage users might figure out ways to swerve these restrictions anyway.

Limits (with caveats): Many of the new safety measures focus on time limits. By default, users under 18 in the US will be blocked from using Meta’s social apps at night and be limited to two hours of scrolling per day. But features like autoplay and algorithmic feeds won’t be disabled by default, though they can be turned off. (There’s also a grab bag of exceptions, like DMs and long-form content—anything of at least 22 minutes—being excluded from the daily use limits.) Parents can also lift or tweak many of these settings.

A big W for Meta?: Crucially, if YouTube, TikTok, and Snap agree to similar restrictions, Meta will set the daily time limit for under 18s in the US to just one hour. The average American teen browses Instagram for about 66 minutes per day, per Meta—lower than what they spend on YouTube (almost two hours) and TikTok (about an hour and a half)—so this would mark a huge win for Zuck’s company.

Bottom line: If Meta can pressure its competitors to adopt comparable measures, it’ll essentially give up six minutes of screen time per user while they lose up to an hour—and it gets to make off looking like the good guy. —WK

item.title: The AI boom’s ROI solution
item.dc:creator: Morning Brew Creative Studio
item.description: Storage is the new backbone of tokenomics.
item.content:encoded:
High-density flash should be a high priority. Solidigm’s eSSDs pack 122TB in a fraction of the space of older drives. Big number of data points that live in a smaller world: smaller footprint, higher efficiency, and higher performance mean ROI is there for the taking. Not to mention, it’s the future. Start thinking data-centric.

A few years into the AI boom, and the math has exploded. Between 2021 and 2023, the scale of AI training datasets skyrocketed. The total volume of training data for notable large language models (LLMs) grew from hundreds of millions to over a trillion data points (tokens), representing an increase of roughly 1,000%–3,000% depending on the specific model, and it continues to grow.1

So what’s one of the most important things to think about when you’re talking about AI infrastructure? Storage—managing AI token consumption, aka tokenomics—and ROI should be top of mind.

It’s all about that storage and the ROI it brings

Storage has graduated from warehouse duty; it’s an extension of accelerator memory itself. Every AI token’s economics get decided below the GPU, and yet, astonishingly, most infrastructures still bolt storage on only after sizing compute. That might be backward these days, especially if you consider that storage has become a day-zero design decision that shapes throughput, latency, and the cost of running AI at scale.

High-density flash solutions now pack more than 5x the capacity of traditional hard drives2 into a deck-of-cards form factor. It’s like having a smaller boat that holds more people than your friend’s bigger boat. It’s (weird) science.

The 10 petabytes you need for your next model could cost you 417 hard drives (HDs). Ouch. But with higher-density solid-state drives (SSDs), that could drop to roughly 84. Less ouch.

And less everything. High-capacity SSDs shrink your storage footprint and power draw per terabyte. That freed-up power and rack space doesn’t vanish; it becomes budget for more GPUs. Better storage = more compute headroom.

Now that should have you thinking about ROI in 3D (you’ll see). SSDs trade higher up-front hardware costs for massive long-term operational savings. They maximize profitability by eliminating costly downtime and accelerating system productivity.

Tokenomics and why the C-suite cares

A thing or two about token pricing (input/output cost per million). Storage lowers both fixed and variable AI costs:

  • Fixed: Reduces training costs (checkpointing, data I/O across GPU clusters).
  • Variable: Reduces per-inference cost at serve time.

Density is a primary lever: Replacing multiple HDs with high-capacity SSDs cuts power, space, and materials, and that can’t be overstated.

ROI has another dimension: What drives tokenomics is output value versus cost.

  • Output value: The services your AI infrastructure delivers—real-time inference, model serving, data retrieval, streaming, rendering. SSDs provide the low latency needed to deliver these services reliably.
  • Production cost: The full stack of keeping models running—compute, storage, power, cooling, and per-token inference across your infrastructure.

Translation: If output value doesn’t beat production cost, you don’t have ROI—you have a token price with its fingers crossed.

Over the last few years, storage tech has evolved from consumer-focused SSDs to enterprise-grade solutions built for data centers and edge environments alike. What started with quad-level cell NAND in 2018 (storing 4 bits per cell instead of 3) has matured through multiple generations. Today’s fourth-gen QLC-based drives cross the 100TB threshold per device, with breakthroughs in endurance and reliability that make them viable for 24/7 workloads.

And speaking of crossing the 100TB threshold, the Solidigm 122TB D5-P5336, the first-to-market SSD to break the 100TB barrier, put the “e” in eSSD. That’s enterprise solid-state drive. In fact, they coined the initialism eSSD. But more than that, when you consider how much storage 122TB holds (the entire collected works of William Shakespeare over 17 million times3), it’s proof that density and efficiency will define who scales profitably in a resource-constrained, heavily regulated world.

Fun and games

At AI Field Day 8 in May, their engineers walked through the anatomy of a single AI prompt to reveal how much storage sits behind responses that feel instantaneous. A single user query balloons into tens of thousands of tokens as context, domain rules, and session history get layered in. Storage assembles this comprehensive prompt before it hits the GPU. By caching stable portions of context, systems convert expensive recomputation into faster reads, freeing GPU cycles and cutting power draw. Like a ripple effect.

And the implications continue to ripple. In one benchmark, extending key-value (KV) cache to non-volatile memory express (NVMe) delivered up to 4x throughput and dramatically improved latency. And on a reasoning-heavy math test, additional output token capacity let models deliberate longer and score higher. Capacity being not merely background infrastructure but part of the answer is what is known in some circles as an attractive return on investment.

The story gets better and broader

Storage tiers now span from fast system memory through local NVMe, in-rack solutions, and network-attached drives. Each layer serves different workloads, from random reads demanding tight latency to bandwidth-heavy ops processing large blocks. The right architecture depends on balancing performance against cost for multi-agent, long-context workloads.

Meanwhile, the physical constraints defining modern AI buildouts are getting stricter. Power availability, sustainability mandates, and footprint limits are less minor concerns and more design challenges. Liquid-cooled form factors, like the world’s first cold-plate-cooled eSSD, and power-sipping optimizations help dense deployments stay viable in regulated environments. Reliability at the edge matters, too, since data doesn’t always stay in a central data center.

The companies pulling ahead are optimizing around their whole systems. And that’s where decades of focused engineering on storage matter.

Smaller is the new bigger

You can think of it as paying for more storage, but more accurately, you’re paying less for everything storage touches, and storage touches everything.

If we do the math, the answer will always be the same. High-capacity SSDs deliver staggering storage density while consuming less space (freeing more space for other stuff) and less energy. The return on investment could trickle down to every other cost factor in the long run. This is the moment for leaders banking that AI’s next chapter doubles down on storage, quietly carrying the load while delivering solid ROI. Decades of innovation, pure-play focus, and end-to-end portfolio—from core data centers to the edge—could make for an obvious choice.

  1. As tracked by epoch.ai
  2. enterprisestorageforum.com/hardware/types-of-computer-memory/
  3. nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/an-example-information-retrieval-problem-1.html

item.title: Bill Gates has a lot to say about AI
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: In a dizzying round of interviews with the media (as well as one very long blog post), Bill Gates is now imploring the world to take the dangers of AI more seriously.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: Bill Gates, in his own words, might now be the “shrillest voice” on AI risk. He’s done a flurry of interviews (which all dropped today) sounding the alarm on a technology he thinks could destabilize the world, posted a 5,900-word blog post on how it could be the “worst source of injustice”—and says he’s been talking about it with leaders in government and the tech industry, too. The question is, will people listen?

What happened: In a wide range of interviews published today, the Microsoft co-founder sent a dire warning about how AI could drive job loss and bioterrorism. And he’s not alone. Behind closed doors, Gates says tech executives are actually “very worried” about AI—but are downplaying it publicly.

The tech billionaire hasn’t exactly embraced the spotlight lately. He acknowledged to Axios that his past relationship with Jeffrey Epstein (which he called a “huge mistake”) could impact how much weight his voice has on the AI debate. But he’s speaking out now because AI has already crossed critical thresholds that make it dangerous. “I am in a state of shock that I’m sort of the first one saying, ‘This is crazy. This is insane,’” he told Semafor (a comment that Dario Amodei might take issue with).

Pathogens and paychecks: During his media tour, Gates zeroed in on the tech’s potential impact on jobs, saying that there won’t be a job left unaffected because humans will eventually be “vastly inferior to the AI doing the job.” And the other thing keeping Gates up at night: he now believes the risk of bioterrorism is about 50 times higher than the risk of a natural pandemic.

How to avoid the bad outcome: The former tech CEO didn’t only throw out bleak forecasts, though. Gates proposes an AI token tax that would make automating roles less financially attractive—and suggests that certain jobs (like athletes and childcare workers) should be “human reserved.” The billionaire also thinks voluntary AI oversight measures are a bad idea and calls for international agreements around AI monitoring: “Self-regulation on the most dangerous tool ever invented?” he said to the NYT. “No, thanks!”

Bottom line: Gates argues that his message might resonate exactly because he’s an unlikely messenger—an “innovation lover” who’s now deeply concerned. Though the fact that he’s an influential billionaire better known these days for his philanthropy than for Microsoft probably doesn’t hurt. —WK

item.title: Cybercab’s big debut
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: Tesla’s Cybercabs will start driving around Austin soon—and it’ll be a big test for its robotaxi business, whose small fleet has logged relatively few unsupervised miles compared to competitors.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: The world’s most sci-fi-looking robotaxi is hitting the roads soon—without a steering wheel or brake pedal. But while Tesla’s been promoting the big public debut of the Cybercab, there are a lot of outstanding questions about how they will actually operate.

What happened: Almost two years after Tesla first revealed the Cybercab, the company’s about to start opening them up to customers. It’s hosting a splashy, invite-only event in Austin on September 3 tied to the robotaxi’s launch, which the company frames as a chance to “experience the future of full autonomy.”

Despite the imminent launch, though, there’s a lot we still don’t know—including how many Cybercabs will be roaming the streets of Austin, and whether Tesla’s nascent robotaxi business is ready to unleash cars that nobody can physically drive.

What we know so far: The Cybercab first drew attention for its distinctive (and polarizing) look, but its unusual design goes beyond the paint color: The car has no steering wheel, brake pedal, or rear window—and it seats just two people. Cybercabs have been spotted on some public roads since about June, often with steering wheels during these test drives (and sometimes, apparently, human supervisors).

Miles to go: It’s unclear whether Tesla is ready to debut unsupervised rides (with only remote monitoring). Tesla launched its robotaxi service about a year ago, but its operation remains minuscule compared to competitors—as of June, it had just 59 total cars in its fleet across three Texas cities. (Waymo, meanwhile, now has nearly 4,000 driverless cars on the road in 15 cities.)

Tesla’s unsupervised robotaxis have so far logged about 380,000 miles across six cities, according to a Tesla earnings call from July. Compare that to Waymo (220 million fully autonomous miles as of March) and Amazon’s Zoox, which makes its own steering wheel-less robotaxi (and now has 3 million miles). Zoox launched with free passenger rides in Las Vegas last September, and recently got the green light to start charging for them.

The full self-driving question: Cybercabs will likely run on some version of Tesla’s Full Self-Driving software—the public version of which still requires “active supervision.” With nobody aboard to do that in Cybercabs, though, Tesla leans on remote operators—who’ve caused several minor crashes themselves.

Bottom line: Next week’s event might answer some questions about this robotaxi’s readiness, but the launch remains a big jump for a business with a tiny fleet and few logged miles. —WK

item.title: The data center political attacks are here
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: As public sentiment on data centers continues to sour, both Democratic and Republican candidates are taking a more oppositional stance to them.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: There might be nothing more politically unpopular right now than being a data center cheerleader. Politicians on both sides of the aisle are taking note—and changing their stance—as the midterm elections approach, while AI companies are desperately trying to buy back some goodwill.

What happened: In an interview this past Sunday, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott declared that AI companies “dug their own grave” amid the data center backlash they’re facing—weeks after he ordered a moratorium on new data center power approvals in the state.

It’s a big shift in tone from a governor who called Texas the “epicenter of AI development” last November. And he’s far from alone: An analysis from The Washington Post shows that American politicians have gotten a lot more negative about data centers since last year. Republican leaders have typically been more welcoming of them than their Democratic counterparts, but a few pro-data center elected officials have either lost their elections or faced recalls in recent months. Now, politicians from both parties are adjusting their stance and ramping up attack ads accusing opponents of being too data center-friendly.

AI’s expensive charm offensive: AI firms, meanwhile, are probably feeling the walls closing in on them. In a private memo that leaked last week, the National Republican Senatorial Committee told AI companies to fix their PR problem, saying they had a “toxic brand.”

To be fair, the industry has been scrambling to improve public opinion—like hosting informational sessions in communities where data centers have been planned. (A recent open house hosted by OpenAI included both job boards and taco bars—and it wasn’t even Tuesday.) Then there’s the throw-money-at-it strategy: Several AI labs have pledged multimillion-dollar investments into data center towns, including Meta’s $1 billion community fund.

The payoff hasn’t come: It’s not clear that the PR blitz is working. A Gallup poll in March showed that 71% of people opposed the construction of data centers in their area. Another survey found that 61% of US adults opposed building them—an increase of 12 percentage points since February and March. As one Democratic pollster told the NYT, the backlash might be about more than just personal impact—it’s a sign of Big Tech disgruntlement more broadly, as data centers are a “physical manifestation” of Silicon Valley excess.

Bottom line: Americans have been loud and clear about being anti-data center. Whether the tech industry can change the public’s great antipathy toward them—not just in time for the midterms, but ever—is still an open question. —WK

Also in data centers…

  • Data centers are about to get a whole lot more expensive for builders and customers, with Nvidia reportedly about to hike the price of servers by more than 15%.

item.title: Protests outside NYC offices of Palantir, Google denounce data centers, facial recognition tech
item.dc:creator: Tricia Crimmins
item.description: The events were part of weeklong anti-Big Tech demonstrations across the US.
item.content:encoded:
Palantir’s unmarked NYC office usually flies under the radar, but it was hard to miss on Wednesday morning when hordes of protesters gathered outside it to condemn the tech company’s work with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The demonstration was a part of a weeklong anti-Big Tech movement percolating across the US, organized by activist groups like Make the Road, United Ratepayers, Food & Water Watch, and People’s Action Institute. “Dump Big Tech” is aimed at tech giants like Palantir, OpenAI, and Google; elected officials in New York, New Jersey, California, Nevada, and Pennsylvania; and data center construction sites in Oregon and West Virginia. The protests point to souring public sentiment surrounding Big Tech, especially ahead of midterm elections.

While each protest is centered on different issues, the event outside Palantir’s offices was squarely focused on the company’s connection with ICE. Speakers at the rally said they’re scared that ICE is using Palantir’s technology to surveil immigrant communities.

“My community has felt a sense of fear that no one should have to feel,” Faith, a youth organizer for Make The Road, an immigrant justice group, told the crowd. (Organizers asked that Faith be identified only by her first name for her safety.) “Palantir working with ICE makes me worry deeply about privacy and about people getting caught up in systems that don’t feel fair, transparent, or humane.”

Because of fears about Palantir using its facial recognition technology against protesters, a majority wore disposable masks, while others wore paper masks decorated with the faces of cartoon characters and superheroes that obscured their entire visage.

“That’s a big fear, that a lot of our data and our identities [will] be tracked by Palantir because we’re here, or because we’re against the violence that ICE is enacting,” Jennifer, a Make the Road organizer who declined to share her surname, told us. “We know that it’s happening across the board, not only to undocumented people. US citizens that are speaking up are being tracked.”

She said she and other protesters hoped the demonstrations encourage elected officials to “look into the contracts” the government has with Big Tech companies and “undo all of the massive surveillance and use of AI that’s only hurting communities.”

NY Assemblymember Claire Valdez, who recently won the Democratic nomination for a US House seat in New York’s 7th Congressional District, also spoke at the rally and offered alternative uses for AI and the advanced technology coming out of companies like Palantir.

“This technology should be used to make our lives better. It should be used to shorten our working hours. It should be used to make our productivity actually pay us more. It should be used to tackle the real emergencies that we are facing right now, like climate change. Instead it is being used by billionaires and tech oligarchs to tear our communities apart,” Valdez said. “We are not going to take it anymore…While Palantir is surveilling us, we are watching them.”

At another demonstration a few blocks away in front of Google’s NYC offices earlier that day, protesters chastised the company for its data centers’ considerable water, energy, and potential fossil fuel usage. Protester Zack Winestine, part of the Rise and Resist direct action group, said he was also demonstrating against “unregulated AI” and Google specifically “forcing people to use AI” when using its search engine.

“AI is not inevitable. There’s all this hype that it can’t be stopped. That’s nonsense. People have agency. People have the right to determine how their lives will be lived and under what circumstances technology functions in their lives,” Winestine told us. “We can affect how these things develop.”

item.title: Google exec says link lists aren’t going away as search transforms
item.dc:creator: Patrick Kulp
item.description: Google VP of Search Liz Reid discussed how the search experience is changing in the AI era and what it means for the internet as a whole.
item.content:encoded:
In recent months, AI has fundamentally changed what it means to google something—and the transformation isn’t done.

The search engine made a slew of announcements at its developer conference earlier this year that included the first change to the search box in a quarter century. The upshot is a more AI-centric experience with options for news alert-style information agents that automatically scour the web for you.

Though Google has clarified that the familiar list of links isn’t going away, multiple headlines have called it the end of search as we know it. But Reid insisted that Google still cares about the health of the internet as a whole.

“Search is not a useful product if the web is not a thriving product, and so I think we probably care about that more than any other company in the world,” Google VP of Search Liz Reid told us.

We spoke with Reid about what this means for how you browse the web, what it means for websites that depend on Google for survival, and how it will change the ads you see.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Do you think that there’s a time in the future, amid all this AI change, that the familiar list of links could go away entirely? Or that there could be a different format for funneling users to the web?

I don’t see any time in which the links go away. I think what we actually see is that people don’t want AI or the web; they want both. There’s a lot of topics where AI really gets you started, and then people want to engage more. They value the expertise, the opinions, the taste of how to think about a particular topic. This is a time in which AI is growing, and it’s a time in which newsletters and podcasts and videos and all these new formats seem to also be blossoming because people really want to hear that expertise. So we want to continue to make that thrive.

We have for a long time continued to innovate on how you can surface links on the web. So we have the blue links, but we have, at times, we have the top stories part. We have what people are saying in AI Mode and in AI Overviews.

If we know users want to connect to that information, how do we make it as easy as possible? How do we make it as seamless as possible? And we’ll continue to innovate and we announced some updates pretty recently on how we’re showcasing links in additional ways. But I think that is kind of what makes search at its heart—not just knowing the information about the web, but connecting people to content on the web. And I don’t see that going away.

Obviously, online publishers are seeing click-through rates decline with these changes, and some publishers are even considering blocking all Google crawlers. In terms of making sure that the open web is still a healthy place to supply these AI tools and search, how do you think about that in the long term?

We do spend a lot of time thinking about this. We try to really design our AI experiences in sort of a web-forward way. We have teams whose job is to think about: What are great links to surface more effectively? How do you show them in a way that’s great for folks? We’ve innovated; one example is in AI Overviews, we’ll now often show on some timely stories, a big carousel of publishers that we didn’t have three months ago. So we’re constantly trying to figure out how we innovate on that.

The good news is that people still want to connect with other people’s content, and so we can facilitate that. And as long as people make great content that other people want to read, then we believe we can continue to foster that.

Companies like Microsoft are experimenting with publisher marketplaces or other compensation schemes. Is that something you’re considering?

We have a blog post in which we’ve talked about some of the various news deals and other things we have.

We have a variety of different ways—we have a long history of deals with news and others for great content. In general, we’re all still—I mean, at times it can feel like a long time—but we’re still pretty early in the space, and so continue to innovate.

In terms of the revenue side, how has this changed Google’s ad model? Do you feel like you’ve kind of cracked advertising in generative AI?

What we are seeing is as people ask longer queries, they’re specifying more of their intent. What are they really trying to do? What’s important to them? And that sort of allows new opportunities to think about ads targeting.

There’s some efforts like direct offers, in which…the advertiser can give a more specific ad for you based on what it is. And so, an example is like you’re searching for a hotel, you’re searching with a family. Maybe a hotel wants to offer free breakfast. They’re not going to give free breakfast to the person that they think is traveling for business who will just pay, or they won’t eat. But this family might pick that hotel because of it, and so Google’s system will allow [the hotel] to say, “Oh, I have a special discount just for you for breakfast,” and that really provides new value to the user and sort of allows the hotel to get additional visitors. We both have something that’s working, and there’s lots of room for innovation going forward.

There’s always been some level of slop on the internet, and I know Google has tools to sift through that. But as generative AI tools have created this ability to churn out more content, how do you make sure that with things like the AI Overviews, the accuracy is maintained? And have you seen the accuracy of those go up overall?

To your point, there’s always been slop. Sometimes people are like, “Oh, there’s now slop on the web.” In my experience, there’s been slop for 20 years. So we have a lot of experience and teams whose job is to ensure that both we’re getting rid of spam and that that rarely surfaces, and that high-quality content continues to surface. And when we do AI Overviews or AI Mode, we actually make use of those underlying search ranking systems so that it’s the highest-quality sites going into AI Overviews. Overall, the quality of the AI Overviews has continued to improve and has improved considerably since we first launched. The models are much better, for one, so that really helps. But also, we’ve just learned a lot and continue to grow on what the techniques are [and] how you work with the models to ensure that you can actually really ground the data in high-quality information.

Are Gemini and AI Mode search still different experiences, or are they converging into the same thing?

We think of them as having two different North Stars. Gemini is really focused on being this assistant, and search AI Mode is really focused on a generative AI search experience. And so for search, that means the importance of connecting to the web is vital. And so the way that we show the web is different…we tend to focus on information use cases more heavily. Versus with Gemini, we’ll focus on a lot of productivity and creativity use cases.

The use cases overlap. We have a view that you should meet users where you are, so you don’t go and say, like, “Oops, you asked the question in the wrong product. Try again.” We will try and answer across both of them the full breadth of questions that come to our products, but we will tune them differently, and really tune search to focus on optimizing for information use cases and optimizing for connecting people to the web.

Where is Google search headed in the long term, and what are some of the biggest ways we can expect it to change further?

There’s a couple of things that we see. Experiences are becoming more personal and custom for you, for each one. It’s not just that you can ask that longer question, but that we start to understand how to make information most useful for you. We see people learn differently. We have people who love videos and people who hate videos. We have people who are experts in the financial jargon and not in the medical jargon. We have people who speak different languages.

And so, with some of the things like generative UI…the job is not just for you to technically access information, but for it to be useful to you—that’s an important part of the mission. How do we present information in ways that are much more useful? That sense of building a thing that feels designed for you, and not just designed for 2 billion people, to make it easier for you to understand and grasp the information will continue.

Also, agents and how they show up in search in terms of just, how do they offload more of the work you don’t want to do? I think people have parts of searching where they enjoy and they’re delighted, and then they have parts of tasks that feel like there’s a lot of toil. And so, how can you offload those parts, and then make it easy for people to spend their time on the things they want to enjoy?

We’ll see that people will ask harder and harder questions. That’s been the evolution of search. You get better at answering the question. They’re like, “OK, I’m gonna raise the bar on you,” and so I think we’ll continue to see people go more and more to, what’s the real question they’re trying to get done, what’s the task they’re trying to get done.
